title: The Facts Fight Back: Setting the Record Straight on Structured Word Inquiry's Claims
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos, in her fifth post on Structured Word Inquiry (SWI), addresses the pattern of cherry-picking among SWI advocates -- attributing to researchers positions that misrepresent or omit their full views on the alphabetic principle. She documents three specific instances: Linnea Ehri's shift on morphology being cited while her unchanged stance on phonics is ignored; David Share's principle of combinatoriality embraced while his recommendation to start with a basic code is omitted; and Kenn Apel's morphological research used without acknowledging his explicit endorsement of the alphabetic principle for beginning readers. Her central argument is that embracing morphology and insisting on the alphabetic principle are not incompatible positions; the question is one of sequencing -- and the research, including from Ehri, Share, Apel, and computational modellers like Seidenberg, consistently places phonological decoding first for beginning readers.
points: The alphabetic principle and morphological awareness are not competing approaches but sequentially complementary ones -- virtually all major researchers cited by SWI advocates (Apel, Share, Ehri, Seidenberg) actually affirm both, with phonological decoding as the entry point.

SWI advocates have developed a pattern of citing researchers selectively: referencing a researcher's morphology work while suppressing their explicit statements about the necessity of phonological decoding for beginning readers.

Beginning spellers rely more heavily on phonological information; experienced spellers shift toward morphological information -- this developmental sequence, well-established in research, is precisely what SWI's instructional sequence disrupts for beginning readers.

A student who cannot decode a word cannot access its meaning to trigger orthographic mapping -- 'There is no comprehension strategy powerful enough to compensate for the fact that you can't read the words' (Anita Archer); the SWI emphasis on meaning-first instruction founders on this prior requirement.

The Linguistic Pathways Framework by Tong and Deacon -- despite being presented by SWI advocates as phonics-free -- explicitly states that 'early aspects of knowledge of orthographic features predict gains in word reading' and identifies phonological decoding as the mechanism through which alphabetic knowledge drives reading acquisition.
quotes: What I have said is very basic: all children need the same types of instruction at the outset; some children will need additional instruction because they are dyslexic... This procedure -- often called 'decoding' -- is essential for beginners, giving them a way to translate print to sound. -- Mark Seidenberg

Morphology matters. A lot. But we need to get morphology instruction right. Many of us have only realized to what extent it matters after discovering the research by Kenn Apel and the advocacy of Peter Bowers. However, there's a huge difference between these two morphology advocates: Kenn Apel accepts the alphabetic principle as a necessary component of beginning reading instruction, and Peter Bowers does not. This is a distinction with a difference.

This is also why the idea that students can simply practise complex skills in their full form from the outset is so misguided. It ignores the basic architecture of learning. It assumes that the mind can cope with fully coupled systems before any subsystems have equilibrated. -- Carl Hendrick

For beginning readers, decoding likely takes precedence in determining reading comprehension as learners focus on mastering phonics to interpret unfamiliar words, ultimately facilitating fluent reading. -- Tong & Deacon
There is no comprehension strategy powerful enough to compensate for the fact that you can't read the words. -- Anita Archer

If we don't face the facts about the best approach to beginning reading, our students will most certainly face the consequences of instruction that is based on an incomplete understanding of the principles that underpin cracking the alphabetic code. They deserve better.
